entries.lesson_core_move: Identify whether a continuous-time signal is periodic or aperiodic by testing for a finite repeating period and linking aperiodicity to the need for Fourier-transform analysis.

sections.section_title: Introduction to Periodic vs. Aperiodic Signals
sections.learning_goal: Define a continuous-time signal as periodic when some finite $T>0$ satisfies $x(t+T)=x(t)$ for all $t$, and use that test to separate periodic from aperiodic signals before choosing Fourier series or Fourier transform.

image_policy.image_description_seed: No image needed; keep the tutorial purely symbolic.
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Do not generate an image. Use only symbolic definitions and a simple sinusoid example.

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: Teach the periodicity test: check whether a finite $T>0$ exists with $x(t+T)=x(t)$ for all $t$, and use that result to decide whether the signal is periodic or aperiodic.
tutorial_outline.base_case: Start with a single sinusoid such as $x(t)=\cos(\omega_0 t)$, where the repeat period is easy to verify and the idea of a smallest positive period is concrete.
paragraph_plan: State the definition of a periodic continuous-time signal using a finite repeating period.
Show the base case of a single sinusoid and how its smallest repeat period is read off.
Contrast a signal that repeats exactly with one that never satisfies the finite-period test.
Connect periodic signals to Fourier series and aperiodic signals to Fourier-transform analysis.
Preview that the next sections will test more complicated signals and then use the classification to choose an analysis method.

sections.section_title: Testing a Signal for a Finite Repeating Period
sections.learning_goal: Test a signal built from multiple sinusoidal terms for a common finite repeat period and decide whether the signal is periodic.

question_policy.answer_format: Choose the correct periodicity classification and, when periodic, a valid finite repeat period.
question_policy.practice_question_model: Given $x(t)=\cos(2t)+\cos(3t)$, determine whether the signal is periodic and choose a valid repeat period if it is.
distractor_plan: Use one component's period as a distractor even though the signal must repeat both components at once.
Include a larger common multiple that is valid but not the best answer if the prompt asks for the smallest repeat period.
Include the other component's individual period as a tempting but incomplete choice.
Include "aperiodic" as the conceptual distractor.

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: Not applicable for an example section.
tutorial_outline.base_case: Not applicable for an example section.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Determine whether $x(t)=\cos(2t)+\cos(3t)$ is periodic, and if it is, identify a valid repeat period.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Show how to test two periodic components for a shared finite period and conclude periodicity by finding a common repeat time.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Moves from one sinusoid in the tutorial to a sum of two sinusoids whose periods must be reconciled into one common finite period.
solution_step_plan: Find the repeat period of each sinusoidal term.
Ask whether both terms repeat at the same finite $T$.
Choose a common finite period that satisfies both repetitions.
State that the signal is periodic and name the period.

Swap sine and cosine terms without changing periodicity.

sections.section_title: Identifying Aperiodic Signals from Failed Period Tests
sections.learning_goal: Recognize that a signal is aperiodic when no finite $T>0$ satisfies the repeat test, even if its pieces are individually periodic-looking.

image_policy.image_description_seed: No image needed; the failure of the period test should be shown algebraically.
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Do not generate an image. Keep the example focused on symbolic frequency comparison.

question_policy.answer_format: Classify the signal as periodic or aperiodic from a failed finite-period test.
question_policy.practice_question_model: Given $x(t)=\cos(t)+\cos(\sqrt{2}t)$, determine whether the signal is periodic or aperiodic.
distractor_plan: Use a finite period from one sinusoidal term as a distractor.
Use a guessed common period that would work only if the frequency ratio were rational.
Include the periodic classification as the opposite of the correct answer.
Include a period that is numerically plausible but does not satisfy both terms.

tutorial_outline.base_case: Not applicable for an example section.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Determine whether $x(t)=\cos(t)+\cos(\sqrt{2}t)$ is periodic.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Show that a finite repeat period would have to work for both components at once, and that the irrational frequency ratio blocks any such period.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Keeps the same repeat-period test but changes one frequency so the component periods are no longer commensurate.
solution_step_plan: Identify the individual component frequencies or periods.
Assume a finite common period exists and impose the repeat condition on both terms.
Show the required period conditions conflict because the frequency ratio is irrational.
Conclude that no finite period exists, so the signal is aperiodic.
practice_variation_axes: Use irrational frequency ratios in different arrangements.
Vary the number of sinusoidal terms while keeping at least one incommensurate frequency.
Ask only for periodic versus aperiodic, not for a specific period.

sections.handoff_notes: Make the failure of the period test explicit and short; do not drift into Fourier-transform algebra yet.

sections.section_title: Introduction to Aperiodic Signals as Infinite-Period Limits
sections.learning_goal: Define the infinite-period limit idea by repeating one signal copy periodically and letting the copies move arbitrarily far apart, so the aperiodic signal is recovered on any fixed finite window.

image_policy.image_description_seed: No image needed; keep the section symbolic-only and text-driven.
image_policy.image_generation_notes: No image needed. Use equations and text only; do not request diagrams or decorative graphics.

question_policy.answer_format: No practice questions for the tutorial step.
question_policy.practice_question_model: Not applicable; this step is direct instruction only.

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: Teach the bridge idea: a periodic extension repeats one signal copy every $T$ units, and as $T$ grows the extension approaches the original aperiodic signal on any fixed finite time window.
tutorial_outline.base_case: One signal copy repeated with a finite period $T$ so the repeated copies are visible before the limit is taken.
paragraph_plan: Open by stating that the lesson bridges aperiodic signals and Fourier-series analysis through a periodic extension with period $T$.
Define the periodic extension idea: repeat one unchanged signal copy every $T$ units and preserve the copy's shape and values.
Explain that increasing $T$ pushes the repeated copies farther apart without changing the local waveform.
State the limit claim on a fixed finite window: as $T\to\infty$, the periodic extension locally recovers the original aperiodic signal.
Close by previewing that this time-domain limit is what makes the Fourier-transform viewpoint natural for aperiodic signals.
display_math_plan: $$\lim_{T\to\infty} x_T(t)=x(t)\quad \text{on any fixed finite time window}$$

sections.section_title: Building a Periodic Extension from One Signal Copy
sections.learning_goal: Construct a periodic extension by repeating one signal copy with period $T$ without changing the copy itself.

image_policy.image_generation_notes: No image needed. Keep the worked example and practice questions text-only and avoid diagram scaffolding.

question_policy.answer_format: Five symbolic text choices; one correct periodic-extension description.
question_policy.practice_question_model: For a signal copy $x(t)$ that is nonzero on $0 \le t < 1$ and period $T=4$, ask which option correctly describes the periodic extension $x_T(t)$.
distractor_plan: Shift the copy by the wrong amount, such as $T/2$ or $2T$, instead of repeating it every $T$ units.
Stretch or compress the copy instead of translating it.
Keep only one copy and forget the repetition across periods.
Alter the copy's amplitude or shape while repeating it.

Write the periodic extension rule using period $T=4$.

Claim that a larger period makes the copies closer together instead of farther apart.

sections.section_title: Introduction to Frequency Spacing in Fourier Series
sections.learning_goal: Define $\omega_0$ as the angular-frequency spacing between adjacent Fourier-series lines and connect larger periods to smaller spacing.

sections.section_title: Introduction to Continuous Frequency
sections.learning_goal: Show that Fourier-series harmonics lie on a discrete frequency grid $\omega_n = n\omega_0$ and that the grid becomes dense as the period $T$ grows.

image_policy.image_description_seed: No image needed; keep the spectrum discussion symbolic.
image_policy.image_generation_notes: No visual object is needed for this tutorial.

question_policy.answer_format: not-applicable

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: Introduce the harmonic-frequency grid $\omega_n = n\omega_0$ with $\omega_0 = \frac{2\pi}{T}$ and show why shrinking $\omega_0$ prepares the move to a continuous frequency variable $\omega$.
tutorial_outline.base_case: Start from one periodic signal with period $T$ so the learner can see that the Fourier-series spectrum is indexed by integers $n$ but located at frequencies $\omega_n$.
paragraph_plan: State that a Fourier series does not use arbitrary frequencies; it gives harmonics at $\omega_n = n\omega_0$.
Show that the spacing between adjacent harmonics is $\omega_0 = \frac{2\pi}{T}$ and tie that spacing directly to the period.
Increase $T$ and explain that the same harmonic labels now sit closer together on the frequency axis.
Name $\omega$ as the continuous frequency variable that will replace the integer index when the spacing goes to zero.

sections.handoff_notes: Keep the explanation short and symbolic; this section should establish the discrete grid before the worked examples take over.

distractor_plan: Include one choice that multiplies by $T$ instead of dividing by $T$.

question_policy.practice_question_model: If the forward transform is applied to $x(t)$, which symbol names the result and what domain does it represent?
distractor_plan: Name $x(t)$ again as the output instead of $X(j\omega)$.
Describe the inverse transform output instead of the forward-transform output.
Treat $X(j\omega)$ as an input rather than the result of the forward transform.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: The pair notation $x(t) \leftrightarrow X(j\omega)$ is shown. If you start from $x(t)$, which symbol is produced by the forward transform, and what domain is it in?
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Read the notation in the forward direction and identify $X(j\omega)$ as the frequency-domain output.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: This example adds directionality: the learner no longer just matches the pair, but reads the transform from signal to spectrum.
solution_step_plan: Start from the given input symbol $x(t)$.
Read the pair in the forward direction.
Identify $X(j\omega)$ as the output of the forward transform.
State that the output is the frequency-domain spectrum.
practice_variation_axes: Keep the same pair but change the wording so the learner must infer the forward direction from context.
Ask for the output domain instead of the output symbol.
Hide the pair inside a short sentence about transform direction.

sections.handoff_notes: Make the direction explicit in the worked example and keep the practice strictly symbolic. The key skill is recognizing that the forward transform sends $x(t)$ to $X(j\omega)$.

sections.section_title: Reading the Inverse Transform Direction
sections.learning_goal: Given $X(j\omega)$ as the input, identify $x(t)$ as the inverse-transform output and read the notation in the spectrum-to-signal direction.

image_policy.image_description_seed: No image needed; the task is to read the inverse direction from notation.
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Keep the section notation-only; no visual support is needed.

question_policy.answer_format: Choose the one option that correctly names the inverse-transform result and its domain.
question_policy.practice_question_model: If the inverse transform is applied to $X(j\omega)$, which symbol names the result and what domain does it represent?
distractor_plan: Name $X(j\omega)$ again as the output instead of $x(t)$.
Describe the forward transform output instead of the inverse-transform output.
Treat $x(t)$ as the input rather than the result of the inverse transform.
Swap the time and frequency domains while keeping the notation otherwise familiar.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: The pair notation $x(t) \leftrightarrow X(j\omega)$ is shown. If you start from $X(j\omega)$, which function do you recover with the inverse transform, and what domain does it live in?
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Read the notation in the inverse direction and identify $x(t)$ as the time-domain output.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: This example reverses the direction from the previous section, so the learner must switch from spectrum-to-signal reading instead of signal-to-spectrum reading.
solution_step_plan: Start from the given input symbol $X(j\omega)$.
Read the pair in the inverse direction.
Identify $x(t)$ as the output of the inverse transform.
State that the output is the time-domain signal.
practice_variation_axes: Keep the same pair but change the wording so the learner must infer the inverse direction from context.
Ask for the output domain instead of the output symbol.
Hide the pair inside a short sentence about recovering the original signal.
Present the inverse direction with the symbols in a different visual order while preserving the same relationship.

sections.handoff_notes: Keep the inversion explicit and avoid any computational work. The only job is to recognize that the inverse transform sends $X(j\omega)$ back to $x(t)$.

sections.section_title: Interpreting a Fourier Transform Pair Table Entry
sections.learning_goal: Interpret a compact transform-pair table entry by mapping the listed $x(t)$ and $X(j\omega)$ to the time and frequency domains and to the forward and inverse transform pair.

image_policy.image_description_seed: No image needed; the task is to interpret a symbolic table entry.
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Keep the worked example and questions text-only; do not introduce a reference image.

question_policy.answer_format: Choose the one statement that correctly interprets the table entry as a time-domain signal paired with a frequency-domain spectrum.
question_policy.practice_question_model: A transform table entry lists $x(t)$ and $X(j\omega)$ as a paired row. Which statement correctly describes the signal, the spectrum, and the transform relationship it summarizes?
distractor_plan: Describe the row as two independent signals with no transform relationship.
Treat both symbols as time-domain quantities.
Treat both symbols as frequency-domain quantities.
Make the row describe only one direction and ignore the paired notation.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: A transform table entry lists $x(t)$ and $X(j\omega)$ as a paired row. Explain what the row says about the signal, the spectrum, and the transform relationship.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Use the compact table entry to recover the same domain match and transform pairing from the earlier examples.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: This final example compresses the same relationship into a table-style reference entry instead of an inline pair or direction prompt.
solution_step_plan: Recognize the row as Fourier pair notation in compact table form.
Map $x(t)$ to the time domain.
Map $X(j\omega)$ to the frequency domain.
State that the row summarizes the forward and inverse transform relationship between the two symbols.
practice_variation_axes: Use a row with the symbols in the opposite visual order while keeping the same pairing.
Ask which column is time domain versus frequency domain.
Ask which symbol should be selected from a reference table when given a plain-language description.
Present the pair inside a compact notation block rather than a table cell.

sections.handoff_notes: Use this section to consolidate the same matching skill in compact reference-table form. The practice should still be symbolic and should test the same domain and direction reading.
